title: Emissions by source and net
summary: Gross emissions are three things added together: what firms release directly in production, what homes release directly (heating and transport: a fixed footprint per person, a larger one for the estate household), and what the power plants release when they burn fuel. The forest then absorbs some, and what is left is net emissions. Electricity use is not counted a second time at the firm or household: it is counted once, at the plant. A private jet flight is a fourth, occasional source (see the private jet topic).
formula: gross = firms (output x intensity x (1 - green tech)) + households (people x footprint; the estate household has its own figure) + private jet flights (tonnes per flight, in the months the jet flies) + plants (fossil energy delivered x emission factor); net = gross - forest sink

params.label: Direct footprint per person
params.unit: t CO2 per person per month

params.label: Emission factor of a fossil plant
Forest sink per unit of standing forest
params.unit: t CO2 per month per unit

examples.label: A Factory making 1,000 units a month with no green technology
The same Factory after 20% green technology
A fossil plant delivering 5 units of electricity in a month
A forest of 1,500 units
examples.note: The sink shrinks as the forest burns or is cleared.

statusNote: Tuned for gameplay. A coal-like emission factor (about 1 t CO2 per MWh) is a rough real-world order of magnitude; the other figures are not calibrated to data.
leavesOut: Only CO2 is counted; no methane, no imports or exports of embodied carbon.
The whole town's footprint is one number; no transport, heating or diet detail.

title: Power: demand, supply and rationing
summary: Firms and households need electricity each month. Each plant has a fixed capacity. If the town wants more than the plants can supply, everyone is served in the same proportion and firms make less. Only fossil plants emit, so the cleaner the plant mix, the lower the emissions per unit of electricity.
formula: demand = firms (output x energy per unit x (1 - green tech) x heat) + households; served = min(1, supply / demand); plant output = delivered x plant capacity / total capacity

params.label: Emission factor of a fossil plant
Extra demand per unit of drought severity

examples.label: Two fossil plants and one renewable plant
A Factory making 1,000 units with 20% green technology

statusNote: The unit is called MWh but the capacities are game numbers chosen so that the starting town is near balance; they are not calibrated to real plants.
leavesOut: No grid: no transmission, storage, imports, prices or blackouts by area.
Plants do not wear out and never run at part load by choice.

title: Grid and energy units
summary: Electricity in the game is counted in MWh per month (the label comes from content). Capacity, demand, deliveries and household use are all in this one unit. Grid intensity is the tonnes of CO2 emitted per unit delivered: the fossil share of capacity times the fossil emission factor.
formula: grid intensity = fossil capacity / total capacity x fossil factor (t CO2 per MWh); renewable share = renewable capacity / total capacity

params.label: Emission factor of a fossil plant

examples.label: One fossil plant of three
An all-renewable grid

statusNote: Unit label only; magnitudes are game numbers.
leavesOut: No distinction between peak and average power, or between electricity and other energy.

title: Household electricity needs
summary: Each household wants a base amount of electricity per person plus an amount that grows with how much it spends. The need is based on last month's consumption. A drought raises it (cooling, pumping). If the grid cannot meet total demand, households are served in the same proportion as firms.
formula: use = heat x people x (base per person + k x spending per person / reference spending)

params.label: Extra need at the reference spending
Extra demand per unit of drought severity

examples.label: A household of 3 spending $6,000 a month in total ($2,000 each)
The same household in a drought of severity 0.5 (heat = 1 + a_e x 0.5)
A household of 2 spending $1,000 a month in total

statusNote: Invented to make households matter for emissions; not from household survey data.
leavesOut: No appliances, heating fuel or cars; one electricity number per household.

title: Accumulated emissions and the carbon budget
summary: Every month's net emissions are added to a running total. The game gives the town a fixed carbon budget for the whole run. The budget left is the budget minus the total so far. Warming is shown as a straight line from the starting temperature to the 1.5 C limit, reaching it exactly when the budget is gone. If cumulative emissions were ever negative they are held at zero.
formula: cumulative = max(0, previous + net emissions); remaining = budget - cumulative; temperature = t0 + (limit - t0) x cumulative / budget

examples.label: After 450 t of cumulative emissions
After 450 t of cumulative emissions
After 450 t of cumulative emissions

statusNote: The budget is scaled down so that a 40-turn game of a 20-person town can use it up. It is not a real-world carbon budget, and the temperature line is a game device, not a climate model.
leavesOut: No carbon cycle, no lag between emissions and warming, no other countries.

title: Household spending and housing
summary: A household spends part of its income and, slowly, some of its wealth. Spending is split between food, goods and services. Households pay rent for their home; when rent is too large a share of income for several months they can be evicted and look for somewhere cheaper. Rents drift up when homes are nearly full and down when they are empty.
formula: spending = propensity (by class) x disposable income + wealth consumption; rent adjusts by a small step when occupancy passes a trigger

params.label: Share of non-food spending going to services
Share of wealth spent each month
Rent share of income that triggers distress
Months of unaffordable rent before eviction

statusNote: Tuned for plausible shares; not calibrated to household budget data.
leavesOut: Nine households and eight homes: no housing market, mortgages, or moving between towns.

title: Production and output
summary: A firm makes output from its capital and from labour. Labour is the sum over its workers of skill times effective hours; effective hours fall with a long commute. The farm also depends on forest and commons health, climate damage and drought. Output is rationed if the grid falls short, and an emissions cap can limit it further.
formula: output = productivity x capital^alpha x labour^beta, then x farm health, x climate factor, x drought factor (farm), x smoke factor, x electricity served

params.label: Farm output exponent on resource health
Farm output lost at the full carbon budget

examples.label: Productivity 1.0, capital 100 units, effective labour 50

statusNote: Standard Cobb-Douglas shape with game-tuned exponents (alpha + beta = 1, constant returns); not estimated from data.
leavesOut: No intermediate goods, no technology choice beyond green investment, no imports.

title: Wages, prices and profit
summary: Firms pay wages first, then the carbon price and profit tax, then dividends to their owners. Wages drift with unemployment (a Phillips-curve style rule) and with skill. Goods prices are cost-plus: each firm moves its price a share of the way toward its unit cost plus a markup every month, and demand does not enter that rule (shortages and gluts change how much a firm hires and makes, not what it charges; see the market price setting topic). A firm that cannot cover wages pays what it can and falls behind.
formula: wage moves by k x (reference unemployment - unemployment); price moves by an adjustment x (unit cost x (1 + markup) - price); profit = revenue - wages - interest - carbon cost - profit tax

params.label: Months of payroll kept as a cash reserve
How strongly buyers favour the cheaper shop

statusNote: Rules of thumb tuned until the town behaves plausibly; not estimated.
leavesOut: No bargaining, unions setting wages directly, or contracts; goods prices do not respond to excess demand (a modelling choice, see the market price setting topic).

title: GDP
summary: GDP is what the town produces and sells in a month, put on a yearly footing. It adds firm sales, investment (capital that firms buy) and government services (public works, upkeep and the job guarantee). The headline figure is real GDP: nominal GDP divided by a price index, so price rises are not counted as growth.
formula: GDP per year = 12 x (firm sales + investment + government services); real GDP = GDP / price index
statusNote: The accounting definition is standard; the model's parts are simplified.
leavesOut: Unpaid work, housework and nature's services are not in GDP (GPI subtracts some of nature's costs).

title: GPI (genuine progress indicator)
summary: GPI starts from GDP and adjusts it for things GDP ignores. It is cut by inequality (a more unequal town counts for less), and by two costs: the social cost of the carbon emitted and the cost of natural capital used up (forest and commons lost). It can be much lower than GDP, or even negative.
formula: GPI per year = GDP x (1 - Gini) - social cost of carbon x 12 x gross emissions - depletion cost x 12 x depletion

params.label: Cost of one unit of natural capital lost

examples.label: GDP of $600,000 a year, Gini 0.3, 12 t gross emissions and 2 units depleted in the month

statusNote: The social cost of carbon is in the range of published estimates; the depletion price and the Gini weighting are game choices.
leavesOut: Leaves out unpaid work, leisure, health and many other items real GPIs include.

title: Wage share and profit share
summary: Wage share is the wages households receive divided by monthly GDP. Profit share is the profit of firms that made a profit divided by monthly GDP. They do not add to one: rent, interest, taxes and government services make up the rest. Both come with the dollar amounts they are made of.
formula: wage share = wages paid to households / GDP; profit share = profits of profitable firms / GDP (both for the latest month)
statusNote: Definitions are standard; the Finance tab also shows a labour-versus-profit split (wages / (wages + profit)), which is a different ratio.
leavesOut: Self-employment and owner income are folded into profit or dividends.

title: Public debt over GDP
summary: Public debt is what the government owes the bank. It is shown over a full year of GDP. When the ratio goes above one, legitimacy starts to drain. The government borrows when it spends more than it collects, within what the bank can lend, and repays part of any surplus.
formula: debt / GDP = government debt / annual nominal GDP

params.label: Share of a surplus used to repay debt
Legitimacy lost per unit of debt/GDP above 1

examples.label: Debt of $300,000 with annual GDP of $600,000

statusNote: Debt is only to the local bank; no bonds, no interest-rate risk beyond the bank's rate.
leavesOut: No foreign lenders, no central bank, no default by the government.

title: Inequality (Gini)
summary: The Gini coefficient measures how unequal wealth is: 0 means everyone has the same, 1 means one person has everything. In the game each person is given an equal share of their household's net worth, then the Gini is taken across all 22 people. The Lorenz curve shows the same thing as a picture. Net worth is savings plus homes and firm shares owned, minus debt.
formula: Gini = sum over all pairs of people of |wealth_i - wealth_j| / (2 x people x total wealth), kept within 0..1

examples.label: Four people holding $10, $20, $30 and $40

statusNote: The formula is the standard one; the wealth sharing inside a household is a simplification.
leavesOut: No income Gini; no distinction between wealth earned and inherited.

title: Legitimacy
summary: Legitimacy is the public's trust in the government, from 0 to 1. At zero the town collapses. Each month it goes up when people are doing well and goes down for high unemployment, high inequality, high public debt, a bank bailout, or switching economic system. Political capital to spend regenerates in proportion to it.
formula: legitimacy = previous + w x (wellbeing - 0.5) - w x max(0, unemployment - threshold) - w x max(0, Gini - threshold) - w x max(0, debt/GDP - 1) - bailout penalty - switching resistance, kept within 0..1

params.label: Political capital regenerated per turn at full legitimacy

examples.label: Wellbeing 0.6, unemployment 15%, Gini 0.5, debt/GDP 1.2

statusNote: Weights are game balance numbers; real legitimacy is not a single number.
leavesOut: No elections, parties or protests; the player simply governs until trust runs out.

title: Bank capital ratio
summary: The bank's capital ratio is its equity divided by its loans. The policy sets a minimum ratio; the bank cannot lend more than its equity divided by that ratio. Headroom is how many dollars it can still lend. A higher required ratio makes lending safer but limits credit and growth.
formula: capital ratio = equity / loans; lending limit = equity / required ratio; headroom = limit - loans

examples.label: Equity of $50,000 with a 10% requirement

statusNote: The idea follows capital rules for real banks; the numbers are game values.
leavesOut: One bank, no depositors who run, no interbank market.

title: Money and credit
summary: Money is bank deposits. When the bank lends, it creates a deposit; when a loan is repaid the deposit disappears. So lending creates money and repayment destroys it. Firms and the government borrow, with interest set by the base rate plus a spread that rises with leverage. Loans that are not repaid for several months are written off and cost the bank equity.
formula: loan rate = base rate + spread (rises with leverage); deposits = money supply; write-off after N months without payment

params.label: Base spread over the policy rate
Extra spread per unit of leverage
Months before a loan is written off
Gap between loan and deposit rates
Share of bank profit paid to its owner

statusNote: The money-creation mechanism follows how banks really work; the rates and terms are game values.
leavesOut: No central bank, no cash, no foreign money, no household credit (switched off).

title: Income tax
summary: Income tax (the lever key is tax_wage) is a flat rate on the wages households earn, including job-guarantee pay and public-works pay. It is collected monthly from savings; a household that cannot pay in full pays what it has.
formula: income tax = rate x wages earned (paid only up to the household's savings)

examples.label: A rate of 15% on $8,000 of wages in a month

statusNote: A flat rate; real income taxes are progressive and have allowances.
leavesOut: No tax-free allowance, no brackets, no tax on pensions separately.

title: Profit tax
summary: Profit tax is charged on a firm's profit before dividends (revenue minus wages, interest and carbon cost). Nothing is charged on a loss. Lobbying by owners can lower the rate in force below the rate you set.
formula: profit tax = effective rate x max(0, revenue - wages - interest - carbon cost)

params.label: Largest share of a policy lobbying can remove

examples.label: A rate of 25% on $4,000 of pre-tax profit

statusNote: A flat corporate tax; no loss carry-forward, depreciation allowances or avoidance.
leavesOut: No loss carry-forward, no tax havens.

title: Capital tax
summary: Capital tax is charged on what households receive from owning things: dividends from firms, rent from homes and interest. It is a flat rate on that income, collected monthly.
formula: capital tax = rate x (dividends + rent received + interest received)
statusNote: A flat rate on capital income; no distinction between kinds of capital income or capital gains.
leavesOut: No capital gains tax, no inheritance tax.

title: Wealth tax
summary: The wealth tax is an annual rate on a household's net worth above a threshold, collected in twelfths each month. Net worth is savings plus homes and firm shares, minus debt. Lobbying can weaken the rate in force.
formula: monthly wealth tax = effective annual rate x max(0, net worth - threshold) / 12

examples.label: A household worth $200,000 with a $100,000 threshold and a 2% annual rate

statusNote: The mechanism is standard; the threshold and rate ranges are game values.
leavesOut: No valuation problems or capital flight: wealth is measured exactly and cannot leave.

title: Carbon price
summary: The carbon price is dollars per tonne of CO2, charged to each firm on its footprint: its direct emissions plus the emissions of the electricity it uses. It reduces profit, so firms invest in green technology and cut output. The price in force can be lowered by lobbying. An emissions cap is a separate limit on a firm's footprint.
formula: carbon payment = effective price x (direct emissions + energy use x grid intensity)

params.label: Green technology gained per investment step

examples.label: A price of $50 per tonne on a footprint of 10 t

statusNote: The mechanism follows a carbon price; the response of firms is a simple rule.
leavesOut: Households do not pay a carbon price on their own footprint.

title: GST / VAT: not modelled
summary: The town has no sales tax. Adding one would change prices, demand and the ledger, so it is a possible future change rather than a setting. The government's tax money comes from income, profit, capital, wealth and carbon taxes.
formula: There is no GST or VAT in the model.
statusNote: Not modelled.
leavesOut: No sales tax, no tariffs, no excise duties.

title: Policy, political capital and lobbying
summary: Each change you make costs political capital and takes a few turns to start. Wealthy owners lobby against some policies: carbon price, profit tax, wealth tax and the emissions cap. The gap between the rate you set and the rate in force is the lobbying effect. Unions push back, and a campaign finance cap limits how much owners can spend. Cancelling a queued change refunds part of its cost.
formula: effective policy = nominal x (1 - net lobbying pressure); cost = base x size of change x (1 + opposition)

params.label: Political capital regenerated per turn at full legitimacy
Share refunded when a queued change is cancelled
Share of income owners spend on lobbying

statusNote: Lobbying strength and costs are game balance, not measured.
leavesOut: No parties, voters or legislature; lobbying is one number.

title: Wages floor, benefits, basic income and job guarantee
summary: The minimum wage sets a floor under what firms pay. Benefits go to unemployed adults and retired people. Basic income goes to every person. The job guarantee employs a share of the unemployed at the minimum wage in government jobs. All are paid monthly from taxes and borrowing; if the treasury cannot pay, payments are cut pro rata.
formula: benefits = amount x eligible people; basic income = amount x people; job guarantee = minimum wage x people in the scheme

params.label: Months of public spending kept in cash

statusNote: Amounts are game values; the schemes follow common designs.
leavesOut: No pensions system, no means testing or administration costs.

title: Public spending, infrastructure and subsidies
summary: The government buys goods and services from firms with the public spending lever (part to the Factory, part to the Shop). It pays upkeep on roads, public housing, power plants and fire stations and pays to build new ones, as wages to households. A green subsidy covers part of firms' green investment. Resilience spending lowers fire and drought risk.
formula: goods bought = spending x (1 - services share); services bought = spending x services share; upkeep = count x upkeep per item

params.label: Share of public spending buying services

statusNote: Costs and upkeep are round game numbers.
leavesOut: No procurement process, no waste, no cost overruns.

title: Economic systems
summary: The town runs under one of three systems: Market, Regulated or Co-op. Each changes which policies are available and how firms are owned and run (for example, worker co-ops share dividends among employees). Switching takes several months, costs political capital and drains legitimacy while it happens. No system gives the state a share of firms.
formula: each system is a set of rules in content/systems/*.json; switching costs political capital and resistance
statusNote: Systems are stylised ideal types, not descriptions of real countries.
leavesOut: No mixed economies in between and no state-owned firms in any system.

title: Class and mobility
summary: A household's class is worked out from where its income comes from and its skills: capitalists and rentiers live mainly on capital income, workers on wages, managers are skilled. Class sets how much of income is spent and how much political power a household has. A skilled household with savings may start a new firm when demand is strong.
formula: class from the share of income that is capital income and skill; political power grows with wealth

params.label: Capital income share that makes a capitalist
Chance of changing class each month

statusNote: Thresholds are game values; class is a label the model derives, not a measured category.
leavesOut: No inheritance, education or social networks.

title: Forest and commons
summary: The forest and the commons are stocks that regrow. The forest also absorbs carbon. The farm harvests both. A commons can be open, managed by the community with a cap, or enclosed by a wealthy owner who charges a fee. Building clears some forest. Health is the stock as a share of its maximum; the farm's output follows the average of the two.
formula: growth = r x stock x (1 - stock / max) - harvest; forest sink = sigma x forest

params.label: Commons harvested per unit of farm output
Forest harvested per unit of farm output
Forest cleared per dollar of building

examples.label: A forest of 1,000 units

statusNote: Logistic growth is the textbook shape; rates are game values.
leavesOut: No species, soils or water; two stocks stand for all of nature.

title: Weather: climate stress, drought and fire
summary: Climate stress is zero until the carbon budget remaining falls to an onset level and then rises to one as the budget runs out. Higher stress makes droughts and forest fires likelier and fiercer. A drought slows the commons, hurts the farm and raises electricity demand. A fire burns forest tiles, spreads to neighbours and costs output and wellbeing nearby. Fire stations and resilience spending cut the risk and the damage. A forecast shows the risk level.
formula: stress = ((onset - remaining share) / (onset - full)) clamped to 0..1, raised to a curve exponent

params.label: Budget share left at which stress begins
Budget share left at which stress is full
Fire spread cut near a station

examples.label: After 450 t of cumulative emissions
After 800 t of cumulative emissions

statusNote: The shape (more extreme weather as the budget runs out) is realistic; the numbers are game values.
leavesOut: No floods, storms or heat deaths; weather is only fire and drought.

title: Wellbeing and unemployment
summary: Wellbeing is a weighted mix of how well a person's consumption meets their needs, whether they have work, whether they are housed, the state of the environment and local smoke, and how secure their finances are. It moves slowly toward its target. Unemployment is the share of people in the labour force without a job; legitimacy uses a smoothed version.
formula: wellbeing target = weighted sum of consumption, employment, housing, environment, security (less commute and smoke); unemployment = (labour force - employed) / labour force

params.label: Spending that meets a person's needs
Weight of the newest month in smoothed unemployment

statusNote: Weights are a design choice; wellbeing is not measured against survey data.
leavesOut: No health, education, community or leisure.

title: Winning and losing
summary: The game lasts a fixed number of turns (each turn is a quarter, so 40 turns is ten years). You lose if the carbon budget runs out, if legitimacy falls to zero, if unemployment rises past the collapse level, or if a bank failure cascades. The first loss ends the game; surviving the last turn is a win, and the results screen scores the run.
formula: outcome = the first of: budget exhausted, legitimacy 0, unemployment above the collapse level, bank cascade; otherwise survived

params.label: Unemployment that, with a failed bank, collapses the town

statusNote: Thresholds are game design.
leavesOut: No partial credit for recovering after a crisis.

title: What this model leaves out
summary: This is a game about trade-offs in a small closed town, not a forecast. It has 20 people in 8 households, three firms, one bank and a government. It leaves out most of what makes a real economy and a real climate complicated, so use it to see how mechanisms interact, not to predict numbers.
formula: (no formula)
statusNote: All values in the game are tuned for play; see each topic for its status.
leavesOut: Trade and other towns: the economy is closed.
Births, deaths, ageing and migration: the population is fixed.
Other greenhouse gases and the global climate system.
Real-world data: nothing is calibrated.
Households' borrowing, housing markets, stock markets and a central bank.
Politics beyond one lever for lobbying and one number for legitimacy.

title: The estate, its jet and its pilot
summary: One very rich household lives on an estate in the south-west corner and owns a private jet and a short runway. Each month the jet flies with a fixed chance, but only while it has a pilot. A flight adds its tonnes to the month's emissions as their own source, and the estate pays the carbon price on those tonnes out of its savings. The estate's other emissions are a fixed figure per month that replaces the ordinary per-person one. The pilot is paid a fixed wage by the estate household; if the estate cannot pay it in full for several months in a row, the pilot is let go and the jet stays grounded until the estate can afford the wages again.
formula: flight = random draw below the monthly chance, and the pilot is employed; flight emissions = tonnes per flight; carbon charge = carbon price x tonnes (capped by the estate's savings); pilot wage = fixed monthly wage, capped by what the estate holds; let go after N months of short pay; rehired when savings cover M months of wages

params.label: Chance the jet flies in a month
Pilot's wage paid by the estate
Months of short pay before the pilot is let go
Months of wages the estate must hold to rehire

statusNote: Game numbers chosen to make wealth, jobs and emissions visible together; not calibrated to data.
leavesOut: Jet fuel, crew other than the pilot, hangar and maintenance costs: a flight costs the estate money only through the carbon price.
Buying or selling the jet, depreciation, more than one flight a month, routes and destinations.
A carbon price on any household's other emissions.

title: Net worth: savings, homes, the bank, the jet and loans
summary: A household's net worth is what it owns minus what it owes, and it is the figure the Gini, the Lorenz curve, the wealth tax and the richest-household share all use. Assets are its savings (deposits at the bank), the homes it owns at their value, its equity in the bank if it owns the bank, and the estate's private jet at its stated value. The liability is the household's own loans. Each person is counted as an equal share of their household. Unpaid rent is not a line: the model records how many months a household has been behind, not an amount owed, so nothing is subtracted for it. The estate's savings are deposits, so they lower the bank's equity; the bank's owner holds that equity as an asset.
formula: net worth = savings + homes owned + bank equity (bank owner) + jet (estate) + firm equity (see the firms topic) - loans owed
statusNote: Values are the model's own books: homes at their set value, the jet at its stated value with no depreciation. Not market prices.
leavesOut: No pensions, human capital, cars or other possessions.
Unpaid rent and other bills owed between households are not tracked as amounts, so they are not in net worth.

title: Net worth: firms owned
summary: A household that owns a firm owns its books: machines and buildings counted at book value (units of capital times the price of a unit), the cash the firm holds, its unsold stock valued at the firm's own price, minus the loans the firm owes. In a worker cooperative the firm's books are shared equally among the households of its workers; a firm owned by the bank counts for the bank's owner, and a firm owned by the state counts for nobody's household net worth. The four firm lines of a statement add up to the firm's equity.
formula: firm equity = capital units x capital price + cash + stock x price - loans; a household's firm lines are its share of that, line by line

params.label: Price of one unit of capital

statusNote: Book value, not what a buyer would pay: a firm's worth ignores its future profits.
leavesOut: No goodwill or market value of a firm; no shares that can be sold.

title: How an economy is coordinated: markets are one way
summary: Resources are scarce, so a society must decide what to produce, how to produce it and who gets it, and the people deciding each know only a small part of what is needed. A coordination mechanism is a way of making those decisions without anyone knowing everything. A market does it with prices: buyers and sellers adjust to what is scarce. Planning or rules do it with an authority that sets quantities, prices or limits (public housing, rationing, the Soviet system). A firm does it with managers directing work instead of buying every step on a market (the point of Ronald Coase). Community rules do it with shared norms and trust (the commons and co-operatives, studied by Elinor Ostrom). Real economies mix all four. A market does not mean capitalism: who owns the firms is a separate question from how decisions are coordinated. In this town goods, jobs, homes and loans are markets with some rules on top; hiring is decided inside the firm; electricity is shared out by a rule; the commons can be run by the community.
formula: Markets: prices signal scarcity. Rules or planning: an authority sets quantities or prices. Firms: managers direct work. Community rules: shared norms manage a shared resource.
statusNote: A teaching frame, not a model rule: it names which mechanism each part of the town leans on.
leavesOut: The model has no centrally planned economy: a planned system, where the Markets view would show shortages and queues instead of price moves, is a later feature.
Real economies are not split cleanly into four boxes; most institutions mix several.

title: How prices are set in this town: cost-plus, not scarcity
summary: Goods and services prices follow costs, not shelves. Every month each firm moves its price a share of the way toward its unit cost (wages plus carbon cost, per unit made) times one plus its markup. Demand never enters that rule. When buyers want more than a shop has, the gap is recorded as unmet demand and the firm responds by hiring and producing more over the next months: the quantity adjusts and the price does not. When stock piles up, the firm hires less. A carbon price therefore passes through to shelf prices even in a slump. Wages and rents are different: a firm's wage drifts with a trend and with unemployment against a reference rate, and the private rent rises while homes are nearly all taken and renters can bear it, and falls otherwise. Loan rates follow the bank's base rate and how much a firm already owes. A textbook market lets every price move with scarcity; this town does not, and that is a modelling choice, not a discovery about the real world.
formula: goods: price moves a share of the way to (1 + markup) x unit cost; labour: wage step = trend + k x (reference unemployment - unemployment), capped; housing: rent up while occupancy is high and burden is low, else down; credit: rate = base + margin + leverage term

params.label: Share of the gap to the target price closed per month
Occupancy at which rents may rise
Rent burden above which rents stop rising

examples.label: A firm whose unit cost is $20 and whose markup is 40 percent of cost
examples.note: The price moves toward this figure whatever buyers want.

examples.label: Unemployment at 15 percent and a trend of 0.2 percent a month

result.unit: change in the wage per month (a share)

examples.note: Above the reference rate, so the wage step is below the trend (and can be negative).

statusNote: Rules of thumb tuned until the town behaves plausibly. Goods prices ignoring demand is a deliberate simplification; changing it is a balance decision (docs/features/markets.md, scope B).
leavesOut: Goods prices do not respond to excess demand or to unsold stock.
No market power, no bargaining, no search costs, no price differences inside a sector other than by shop.

title: The goods, food and services markets
summary: Households must eat: each person needs a set amount of food a month and spends on it first. What is left after food, and after saving, is split between goods and services. Firms buy machinery from the Factory and the government buys goods and services too. All of this is a budget set before looking at any shop. The budget is then shared out among the sector's shops, favouring those with more stock and lower prices, in two passes so that nobody buys more than a shop has. What buyers would have bought is demand; what was bought is sales; the difference is what went without, and stock minus sales is what stayed unsold. The sector has one shop in this town, so a gap is all or nothing.
formula: demand units = budget share / price; sold = min(demand, stock) over two passes; unmet = demand - sold; unsold = stock - sold

params.label: Food each person needs a month
Share of spare spending that goes to services
How strongly buyers favour the cheaper shop

statusNote: Household budgets are rules of thumb by class. Only the shop split uses a price response.
leavesOut: No shopping around between towns, no brands, no queueing: unmet demand simply goes without.

title: The labour market
summary: Each firm decides how many people it wants from the sales it expects and its stock (a decision made inside the firm, by managers). The gap between that headcount and who it already employs is its job openings. Unemployed people apply to firms with openings, the cheapest first, and a firm hires at most a few people a month, so an opening can stay open while people are out of work. A firm lets people go only after months of sustained surplus. The government's job guarantee employs a share of those left without a firm job. The wage drifts with a trend and with unemployment against a reference rate.
formula: openings = target headcount - current workers; hires = min(openings, monthly cap, people available); wage step = trend + k x (u_ref - u)

params.label: Most people a firm hires in a month

statusNote: Rules of thumb tuned to behave plausibly.
leavesOut: No job search effort, no vacancies posted for skills the unemployed lack beyond a two-tier skill split, no quitting for a better job.

title: The housing market
summary: Each household needs one home. Households without a home, richest first, move into the cheapest empty home whose rent is within a share of their income; a household that falls months behind on rent loses its home (an evicted household does not move at once). Private rent rises while almost every home is occupied and renters spend less than a cap of their income on rent, and falls otherwise. Public rent is a policy lever set by the government, a rule rather than a market price.
formula: rent up if occupancy >= trigger and mean burden < cap, else down; burden = private rent / renters' disposable income

params.label: Occupancy at which rents may rise
Rent burden above which rents stop rising
Largest share of income a household will spend on rent when moving

statusNote: Rules of thumb; there is no bidding between households for the same home.
leavesOut: No building by developers in response to rents, no mortgages, no moving between towns.

title: The credit market
summary: Firms ask the bank for loans when their investment plan needs more than they have. The bank may lend up to its capital divided by the required capital ratio, minus what it has already lent, and no single firm may owe more than a share of what it owns. A request is the firm's plan after its investment rule, not a free wish to borrow. The loan rate is the base rate plus a fixed margin plus a margin that grows with how much the firm owes; it is not raised to ration loans, so when the bank runs short of room it simply lends less.
formula: approved = min(request, bank headroom, firm's leverage limit); rate = base + spread + leverage x leverage margin + system credit spread

params.label: Fixed margin over the base rate
Extra margin per unit of leverage
Most a firm may owe, as a share of what it owns

statusNote: Rules of thumb; the bank does not assess individual projects.
leavesOut: No credit rating, no collateral choice, no loans to households beyond the existing ones.

title: The electricity market (a quantity limit, no price)
summary: Firms and households want electricity every month; the power plants can supply only their capacity. If demand is higher than capacity, everyone is served in the same proportion and output is cut back accordingly. There is no price for electricity in this model: it is shared out by a rule, not by bidding. The commons is the other resource with no price: it is governed by access rules and regrowth, and is shown under Ecology, not here.
formula: served = min(1, capacity / demand); delivered = demand x served
statusNote: A quantity constraint, not a price model.
leavesOut: No electricity price, no storage and no imports.
